money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The local currency is the Peruvian Nuevo Sol (PEN). Declare all amounts more than of $US10,000 in any currency on arrival. laws.rule: Children under 18 years old travelling on an Australian passport must obtain written permission (Autorización de Viaje Notarial) from the non-travelling parent(s) to leave the country. This applies if they have resident status or have stayed in Peru for over 183 days in one year. For more information, see the Peruvian government's website.
laws.heading: Travelling with children

laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe. They include lengthy prison sentences. Prison conditions in Peru are challenging. Don't carry or use illegal drugs. Trained staff use technology to detect illegal drugs at Lima's International Airport and throughout Peru. Australians have been jailed for long periods for drug offences.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: You must carry photo identification at all times. The Peruvian Police may ask to see it. Failure to show identification may result in detention.
laws.heading: Proof of identity

laws.rule: It's illegal to photograph military or police sites and personnel. Indecent behaviour, such as not showing respect at cultural, historical or sacred sites, is against the law. Australians have been detained for this. It's illegal to export handicrafts or goods of cultural or historical significance. If you want to buy or export copies of these, you'll need permission from the Ministry of Culture. It's also illegal to export antiques and artefacts from pre-colonial Peru. If you want to buy and export a reproduction, use a reputable dealer with the right documents. Do not leave Peru with coca leaves, coca tea bags or similar products. It is illegal to remove certain fauna and flora items from
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: You can use your Australian driver's license to drive in Peru for the duration of a tourist visa (maximum 183 days in one year). If you're staying in Peru longer, you'll need an International Driving Permit (IDP).
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: When entering or leaving Peru, declare cash or negotiable instruments (travellers' cheques, bearer cheques) worth more than US$10,000 or the equivalent in any currency. Carrying more than US$30,000 in or out is not permitted. US$10,000 is about A$14,200 (RBA 30 Oct 2026: A$1 = USD 0.7040).
laws.penalty_signal: Leaving out or falsifying the declaration: all the money is held temporarily and a penalty of 30% of the undeclared value applies, with civil or criminal action possible

laws.rule: Duty-free for travellers over 18: up to 3 litres of liquor, and up to 20 packs of cigarettes, or 50 cigars, or 250 grams of cut tobacco. Medicines for the traveller's personal use are among the items that can come in as baggage.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: Law 30740 and its regulation give MTC's DGAC the role of issuing operator or pilot licences for non-recreational RPAS use (recreational drones under 2 kg excluded). Registration is online. No foreign-operator provision found.

items.text: Not yet checked: no public DGAC directory of RPAS operators was found on the pages read.

Anyone operating an RPAS for other than recreational or sport use needs an operator or pilot licence from DGAC; recreational aircraft under 2 kg are excluded. The pilot must be an adult and pass a knowledge exam with at least 75%. Flights over urban areas need an authorisation with a risk analysis, registration card, liability policy and pilot accreditation (decision within 60 working days). RPAS may not operate in controlled airspace.

Not yet checked: whether a foreign pilot can be accredited in Peru. The regulation says operations that cross part of another state's airspace need that state's authorisation. DGAC contact: rpas-dgac@mtc.gob.pe.
